text: Chapter four moves to the open-source stack most teams actually run day to day: Prometheus and Grafana. Before any dashboards, you need Prometheus's mental model — because it's built differently than Azure Monitor or CloudWatch, and that difference shapes everything else in this chapter, from how you write queries to how you set up alerts.

Azure Monitor and CloudWatch are push-based — your application or an agent sends metrics out to the platform. Prometheus flips that around: the server scrapes a metrics endpoint on your application over plain HTTP, on a schedule, usually every fifteen to thirty seconds. That means Prometheus itself notices immediately when a target stops responding, instead of you having to notice a silence in your data later.

Here's the core loop: Prometheus pulls metrics from instrumented applications and exporters, stores them in its own purpose-built time-series database, and pushes any firing alerts on to Alertmanager for routing. Every piece in this diagram gets its own dedicated lesson somewhere in this chapter.

Four pieces make this work. The server scrapes, stores, and evaluates your queries and alert rules continuously. The TSDB indexes everything by metric name and labels for fast lookups, even across millions of time series. Exporters expose metrics for things you can't instrument directly, like a database or the operating system itself. And service discovery finds Northbridge's checkout pods automatically on Kubernetes as they're created and rescheduled — no static IP list to maintain by hand.

That's the architecture: pull, store, discover, alert. One exception worth knowing — the Pushgateway, built for short-lived batch jobs that would finish and exit before a normal scheduled scrape ever caught them. Next up, lesson fifteen — instrumenting an application yourself with counters, gauges, and histograms.
